blocks.value: Workflow Automation with gh

gh excels in CI/CD pipelines and automation scripts. It can create releases, upload assets, manage deployments, and trigger workflows. In GitHub Actions, gh is pre-installed and pre-authenticated with the GITHUB_TOKEN, making it ideal for release automation, issue triage, and cross-repository operations. Shell scripts combining gh, jq, and standard Unix tools can replace complex custom applications for many GitHub automation needs.

# RELEASE AUTOMATION SCRIPT
#!/bin/bash
set -e

VERSION=$1
if [ -z "$VERSION" ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <version>"
  exit 1
fi

# Generate release notes from PRs
NOTES=$(gh pr list --state merged --json number,title,author |
  jq -r '.[] | "- #\(.number): \(.title) by @\(.author.login)"')

# Create release with auto-generated notes fallback
gh release create "$VERSION" \
  --title "Release $VERSION" \
  --notes "$NOTES" \
  --generate-notes

# Build and upload assets
npm run build
gzip -c dist/app.js > dist/app.js.gz
gh release upload "$VERSION" dist/app.js dist/app.js.gz

echo "Release $VERSION published!"

# ISSUE TRIAGE SCRIPT
#!/bin/bash
# Close stale issues with no activity in 6 months

gh issue list --repo owner/repo --state open --json number,updatedAt,title |
  jq -r '.[] | select(.updatedAt < (now - 15552000 | todateiso8601)) | .number' |
  while read -r issue_num; do
    echo "Closing stale issue #$issue_num"
    gh issue close "$issue_num" --comment "Closing due to inactivity. Please reopen if still relevant."
  done

# DEPLOYMENT NOTIFICATION
#!/bin/bash
ENV=$1
VERSION=$2

gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/deployments -X POST \
  -f ref="$VERSION" \
  -f environment="$ENV" \
  -f auto_merge=false

# Notify team
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues -X POST \
  -f title="Deployed $VERSION to $ENV" \
  -f body="Deployment completed successfully." \
  -f labels[]=deployment

parts.partTitle: Part 17: Git Hooks — Automating Your Workflow

blocks.value: Understanding Git Hooks

Git hooks are scripts that run automatically at specific points in the Git lifecycle. They live in .git/hooks/ and are not version-controlled by default (though you can symlink them from the repository). Hooks enable automation: run tests before committing, validate commit messages, prevent secrets from being committed, update issue trackers after push, or notify team chat on deployment. There are client-side hooks (run on your machine) and server-side hooks (run on the Git server). Client-side hooks include pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit, pre-rebase, post-checkout, post-merge, and pre-push. Server-side hooks include pre-receive, update, and post-receive.

# See available hooks
ls .git/hooks/
# Sample hooks (with .sample extension):
# applypatch-msg.sample  pre-commit.sample         pre-rebase.sample
# commit-msg.sample      pre-merge-commit.sample   pre-receive.sample
# fsmonitor-watchman.sample  pre-push.sample       prepare-commit-msg.sample
# post-update.sample     pre-applypatch.sample     push-to-checkout.sample
# update.sample

# Enable a hook by removing .sample and making it executable
cp .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

# Hooks are just executable scripts — any language works:
# Bash, Python, Ruby, Node.js, Go, etc.

# HOOK EXECUTION ORDER:
# 1. pre-commit      — Before commit is created (lint, tests)
# 2. prepare-commit-msg — Edit default commit message
# 3. commit-msg      — Validate commit message format
# 4. post-commit     — After commit is created (notifications)
# 5. pre-push        — Before pushing to remote (integration tests)
# 6. post-checkout   — After branch switch or clone
# 7. post-merge      — After merge completes
# 8. pre-rebase      — Before rebase starts

# Exit code matters:
# - Exit 0 = allow the operation to continue
# - Exit non-zero = abort the operation

# Hooks do not propagate — each developer must install them
# Solution: Use a framework like Husky or Lefthook
blocks.output: Git hooks overview, available hooks, execution order, and activation process.

blocks.value: Practical Hook Implementations

Real-world hooks solve real problems. A pre-commit hook prevents bad code from entering history by running linters and tests on staged files. A commit-msg hook enforces conventional commit format. A pre-push hook runs the full test suite before allowing pushes to shared branches. These hooks catch errors early, when they are cheapest to fix, and enforce team standards without manual policing.

# .git/hooks/pre-commit
#!/bin/bash
# Run linter on staged files only

echo "Running pre-commit checks..."

# Get list of staged files
STAGED_FILES=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep '\.js$')

if [ -n "$STAGED_FILES" ]; then
  echo "Linting JavaScript files..."
  echo "$STAGED_FILES" | xargs npx eslint
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "ESLint failed. Fix errors before committing."
    exit 1
  fi
fi

# Run tests related to staged files
STAGED_FILES=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM)
if [ -n "$STAGED_FILES" ]; then
  echo "Running related tests..."
  npm test -- --findRelatedTests $STAGED_FILES --passWithNoTests
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "Tests failed. Fix before committing."
    exit 1
  fi
fi

# Check for secrets (simple grep — use detect-secrets for production)
if git diff --cached | grep -E '(password|secret|api_key)\s*[=:]\s*["\'][^"\']+'; then
  echo "WARNING: Possible secrets detected in staged changes!"
  echo "Use 'git commit --no-verify' to bypass (not recommended)."
  exit 1
fi

echo "Pre-commit checks passed!"
exit 0

# .git/hooks/commit-msg
#!/bin/bash
# Enforce conventional commit format

COMMIT_MSG_FILE=$1
COMMIT_MSG=$(head -n 1 "$COMMIT_MSG_FILE")

# Pattern: type(scope): description
# Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore
PATTERN="^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|test|chore)(\(.+\))?: .+"

if ! echo "$COMMIT_MSG" | grep -qE "$PATTERN"; then
  echo "Invalid commit message format."
  echo "Expected: type(scope): description"
  echo "Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore"
  echo "Example: feat(auth): add OAuth2 login"
  exit 1
fi

# Check message length (subject should be <= 72 chars)
if [ ${#COMMIT_MSG} -gt 72 ]; then
  echo "Commit message subject too long (${#COMMIT_MSG} > 72 chars)"
  exit 1
fi

exit 0

# .git/hooks/pre-push
#!/bin/bash
# Run full test suite before pushing to protected branches

protected_branches="main master develop"
current_branch=$(git symbolic-ref HEAD | sed 's!refs/heads/!!')

if echo "$protected_branches" | grep -qw "$current_branch"; then
  echo "Pushing to protected branch '$current_branch'. Running full tests..."
  npm run test:ci
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "Tests failed. Push aborted."
    exit 1
  fi
  
  echo "Running security audit..."
  npm audit --audit-level=moderate
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "Security audit failed. Fix vulnerabilities before pushing."
    exit 1
  fi
fi

exit 0

blocks.value: Husky and Lefthook: Managing Hooks at Scale

Manually installing hooks in .git/hooks/ does not scale — new team members must remember to set them up, and hooks are not version-controlled. Husky (for Node.js projects) and Lefthook (language-agnostic, faster) solve this by storing hook configurations in the repository and installing them automatically on npm install or a setup script. These tools support running multiple commands in parallel, conditional execution, and integration with lint-staged for running linters only on changed files.

blocks.output: Husky and Lefthook configurations for version-controlled, team-shared hooks.

blocks.value: Server-Side Hooks: Enforcing Rules on the Server

Server-side hooks run on the Git server (GitHub, GitLab, or self-hosted) and enforce rules for all clients. pre-receive runs once per push and can reject the entire push. update runs once per ref being updated and can accept/reject individual branches. post-receive runs after the push is accepted and is used for notifications and deployments. On GitHub, server-side hooks are replaced by branch protection rules, required status checks, and GitHub Actions. For self-hosted Git servers (Gitea, Gogs, bare repos), you can implement custom pre-receive hooks for organization-specific policies.

# Self-hosted Git server: pre-receive hook
# Located at: repository.git/hooks/pre-receive

#!/bin/bash
# Reject pushes that contain secrets or violate policies

while read oldrev newrev refname; do
  # Only check main branch
  if [ "$refname" != "refs/heads/main" ]; then
    continue
  fi
  
  # Check for large files (>10MB) being added
  large_files=$(git diff-tree -r -M --no-commit-id --name-only $oldrev $newrev | \
    while read file; do
      size=$(git cat-file -s "$newrev:$file" 2>/dev/null)
      if [ "$size" -gt 10485760 ]; then
        echo "$file ($((size/1024/1024))MB)"
      fi
    done)
  
  if [ -n "$large_files" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: Large files detected (max 10MB):"
    echo "$large_files"
    echo "Use Git LFS for large files."
    exit 1
  fi
  
  # Check commit messages for required ticket references
  commits=$(git rev-list $oldrev..$newrev)
  for commit in $commits; do
    msg=$(git log --format=%s -n 1 $commit)
    if ! echo "$msg" | grep -qE '(JIRA-\d+|#[0-9]+)'; then
      echo "ERROR: Commit $commit missing ticket reference"
      echo "Message: $msg"
      echo "Required format: JIRA-123 or #42"
      exit 1
    fi
  done
done

exit 0

# GitHub equivalent (no server hooks, use Actions instead):
# .github/workflows/enforce-policies.yml
name: Enforce Policies
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0  # Full history for commit checking
      
      - name: Check commit messages
        run: |
          git log --format=%s origin/main..HEAD | while read msg; do
            if ! echo "$msg" | grep -qE '(JIRA-\d+|#[0-9]+)'; then
              echo "Commit missing ticket: $msg"
              exit 1
            fi
          done
      
      - name: Check for large files
        run: |
          find . -type f -size +10M | grep . && \
          echo "Large files found. Use Git LFS." && exit 1 || true

parts.partTitle: Part 18: Advanced Git Configuration and Customization

blocks.value: Git Configuration Files and Hierarchy

Git reads configuration from three levels: system (/etc/gitconfig or C:\Program Files\Git\etc\gitconfig) affects all users on the machine; global (~/.gitconfig or %USERPROFILE%\.gitconfig) affects your user account; and local (.git/config within each repository) affects only that repository. Local settings override global, which override system. Additionally, Git 2.13+ supports conditional includes — you can include different configurations based on the repository path, enabling work/personal separation or per-project settings without manual switching.

# View all configuration with source locations
git config --list --show-origin --show-scope
# Output:
# system  file:/etc/gitconfig       core.editor=vim
# global  file:/home/user/.gitconfig user.name=Your Name
# local   file:.git/config          remote.origin.url=...

# System-level configuration (requires sudo)
sudo git config --system core.editor vim
sudo git config --system init.defaultBranch main

# Global configuration (per user)
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your@email.com"

# Local configuration (per repository)
git config --local user.email "work@company.com"
git config --local core.hooksPath .githooks/

# Conditional includes (Git 2.13+)
# ~/.gitconfig
[user]
  name = Personal Name
  email = personal@email.com

[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
  path = ~/.gitconfig-work

[includeIf "gitdir:~/opensource/"]
  path = ~/.gitconfig-oss

# ~/.gitconfig-work
[user]
  email = work@company.com
[core]
  sshCommand = ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa_work

# ~/.gitconfig-oss
[user]
  email = opensource@email.com
[commit]
  gpgsign = true

# Verify which config applies to current repo
git config --show-origin user.email

blocks.value: Powerful Git Aliases

Git aliases are shortcuts for frequently used commands or complex command combinations. They are defined in your Git config and can be simple command substitutions or complex shell scripts. Well-designed aliases save hundreds of keystrokes per day and make common operations effortless. The ! prefix indicates a shell command, allowing aliases to pipe multiple Git commands, use grep, or invoke external tools.

# Essential aliases to add to ~/.gitconfig

# View current aliases
git config --get-regexp '^alias\.'

# BASIC SHORTCUTS
git config --global alias.st 'status -sb'
git config --global alias.co 'checkout'
git config --global alias.br 'branch -v'
git config --global alias.ci 'commit'
git config --global alias.cim 'commit -m'
git config --global alias.ciam 'commit -am'
git config --global alias.amend 'commit --amend --no-edit'
git config --global alias.unstage 'restore --staged'
git config --global alias.last 'log -1 HEAD --stat'

# ENHANCED LOGGING
git config --global alias.lg "log --color --graph --pretty=format:'%Cred%h%Creset -%C(yellow)%d%Creset %s %Cgreen(%cr) %C(bold blue)<%an>%Creset' --abbrev-commit"

git config --global alias.lg2 "log --graph --abbrev-commit --decorate --format=format:'%C(bold blue)%h%C(reset) - %C(bold green)(%ar)%C(reset) %C(white)%s%C(reset) %C(dim white)- %an%C(reset)%C(bold yellow)%d%C(reset)' --all"

git config --global alias.ls 'log --oneline --graph --all --decorate'

# HISTORY INSPECTION
git config --global alias.hist 'log --pretty=format:"%h %ad | %s%d [%an]" --graph --date=short'

git config --global alias.who "log --pretty=format:'%Cgreen%an%Creset | %s' --shortstat"

# DIFF AND COMPARE
git config --global alias.d 'diff'
git config --global alias.ds 'diff --staged'
git config --global alias.dw 'diff --word-diff'
git config --global alias.dc 'diff --cached'

# BRANCH MANAGEMENT
git config --global alias.b 'branch -a'
git config --global alias.bd 'branch -d'
git config --global alias.bD 'branch -D'
git config --global alias.bm 'branch -m'
git config --global alias.merged 'branch --merged'
git config --global alias.nomerged 'branch --no-merged'

# STASH SHORTCUTS
git config --global alias.sl 'stash list'
git config --global alias.sa 'stash apply'
git config --global alias.sp 'stash pop'
git config --global alias.ss 'stash show -p'

# SHELL COMMAND ALIASES (prefix with !)

git config --global alias.wipe '!git add -A && git commit -qm "WIPE SAVEPOINT" && git reset HEAD~1 --hard'

blocks.value: Customizing Git Output and Behavior

Git is highly customizable beyond aliases. You can configure default behaviors, output colors, merge strategies, diff tools, and more. The core.pager setting controls how long output is displayed (less by default). The color.ui setting enables colored output. The push.default setting controls what git push does without arguments. The merge.conflictStyle setting changes how conflict markers are displayed. Custom diff and merge tools (like VS Code, Beyond Compare, or vimdiff) provide visual conflict resolution. These settings make Git feel like your tool, not a generic utility.

# PAGER CONFIGURATION
# Disable pager for specific commands
git config --global pager.log false
git config --global pager.diff false
# Or use cat for all short output:
git config --global core.pager cat

# COLOR CONFIGURATION
git config --global color.ui auto
git config --global color.status.added green
git config --global color.status.changed yellow
git config --global color.status.untracked red

# PUSH BEHAVIOR
git config --global push.default simple
# simple: push current branch to upstream branch of same name
# current: push current branch to branch of same name on remote
# upstream: push to upstream branch (may be different name)
# matching: push all branches with matching names on remote (dangerous!)

# PULL BEHAVIOR
git config --global pull.rebase true
# Always rebase on pull instead of merge

git config --global rebase.autoStash true
# Automatically stash uncommitted changes before rebase

# MERGE CONFIGURATION
git config --global merge.conflictStyle diff3
# Shows common ancestor in conflict markers:
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# your version
# ||||||| base
# common ancestor
# =======
# their version
# >>>>>>> branch

git config --global merge.tool vscode
git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait $MERGED'

git config --global diff.tool vscode
git config --global difftool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait --diff $LOCAL $REMOTE'

# Enable difftool by default
git config --global diff.external difft

# RERERE: Reuse Recorded Resolution
git config --global rerere.enabled true
# Automatically resolves conflicts using previous resolutions
# Invaluable for rebasing long-lived feature branches

# AUTO-CORRECT TYPOS
git config --global help.autocorrect 20
# Git will run the corrected command after 2.0 seconds
# Example: git sttus -> git status (after 2 sec delay)

# TEMPLATE FOR COMMIT MESSAGES

# ~/.gitmessage:
# Subject line (50 chars)
#
# Body explaining WHY (72 chars per line)
#
# - Bullet points for details
# - Reference issues: Fixes #123

blocks.value: Git Attributes: Per-File Configuration

The .gitattributes file specifies how Git should handle individual files or file patterns. It controls line endings (critical for cross-platform teams), merge strategies, diff behavior, and filtering. blocks.value: Authentication and Permission Errors

Authentication errors are the most common Git problems, especially for beginners transitioning from HTTPS to SSH or managing multiple GitHub accounts. The key is understanding that Git uses different credential helpers for HTTPS (which stores tokens) and SSH (which uses key pairs). When you see 'Permission denied' or 'Authentication failed', the cause is usually an expired token, missing SSH key, wrong remote URL, or credential helper caching an old password.

# ERROR: remote: Permission to user/repo.git denied to user
# CAUSE: Wrong authentication method or insufficient permissions

# Diagnose remote URL
git remote -v
# If HTTPS: https://github.com/user/repo.git
# If SSH: git@github.com:user/repo.git

# FIX 1: Switch from HTTPS to SSH (recommended)
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git
# Ensure SSH key is added to ssh-agent:
ssh-add -l
# If empty: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# FIX 2: Update HTTPS credentials (personal access token)
git credential reject
# Then push again — Git will prompt for new token
# Or update stored credential:
git config --global --unset credential.helper
git config --global credential.helper cache
# Push and enter new token when prompted

# FIX 3: Check token permissions
# GitHub Settings -> Developer settings -> Personal access tokens
# Ensure token has 'repo' scope for private repos

# ERROR: fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com'
# CAUSE: Git cannot prompt for credentials in non-interactive mode
# FIX: Use credential helper or SSH

# ERROR: ssh: connect to host github.com port 22: Connection refused
# CAUSE: Firewall blocks port 22
# FIX: Use SSH over HTTPS port (443)
# ~/.ssh/config:
Host github.com
  Hostname ssh.github.com
  Port 443
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# Multiple GitHub accounts (work and personal)
# ~/.ssh/config:
Host github-personal
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_personal

Host github-work
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work

# Usage:
git clone git@github-personal:personal/repo.git
git clone git@github-work:company/repo.git

# Conditional Git config for different directories (Git 2.13+)
# ~/.gitconfig:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
  path = ~/.gitconfig-work
# ~/.gitconfig-work:
[url "git@github-work:"]
  insteadOf = git@github.com:

blocks.value: Merge Conflicts and History Problems

Merge conflicts, divergent branches, and history mismatches cause significant frustration. The key is understanding what state your repository is in and having a recovery plan. When Git says 'Your branch and origin/main have diverged', it means both you and someone else have made commits on the same branch. When Git says 'fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories', you are trying to merge two repositories with no common ancestor. When Git says 'error: you need to resolve your current index first', you are in the middle of a merge or rebase and must finish or abort it before doing anything else.

# ERROR: Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged
# CAUSE: Remote has commits you don't have, and you have local commits

# FIX 1: Pull with rebase (recommended for local branches)
git pull --rebase origin main

# FIX 2: Pull with merge (creates merge commit)
git pull origin main

# FIX 3: Fetch and inspect before deciding
git fetch origin
git log --oneline --graph --left-right HEAD...origin/main
# Shows which commits are only on your branch vs only on remote

# ERROR: fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories
# CAUSE: Merging two repos with no common commits
# FIX: Force merge (use with caution!)
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories

# ERROR: error: you need to resolve your current index first
# CAUSE: Stuck in middle of merge/rebase/cherry-pick

# Diagnose current state
git status

# If merge in progress:
git merge --abort  # or resolve conflicts and git add + git commit

# If rebase in progress:
git rebase --abort  # or resolve conflicts and git rebase --continue

# If cherry-pick in progress:
git cherry-pick --abort  # or resolve and git cherry-pick --continue

# If bisect in progress:
git bisect reset

# ERROR: fatal: not a git repository
# CAUSE: Not in a Git repo or in a subdirectory without .git
# FIX: cd to correct directory or git init

# ERROR: The following untracked working tree files would be overwritten
# CAUSE: Checkout would overwrite files that exist but are untracked
# FIX: Stash or remove the files, then checkout
git stash push --include-untracked
git checkout main

# ERROR: pathspec 'branch-name' did not match any file(s) known to git
# CAUSE: Typo in branch name, or branch only exists on remote
# FIX: Fetch remote branches
git fetch origin
git branch -r  # List remote branches
git checkout -b branch-name origin/branch-name

blocks.value: Recovering from Disasters

Even experienced developers make mistakes: accidentally deleting a branch, force-pushing to the wrong branch, losing commits after a bad reset, or committing sensitive data. Git's reflog and object database make most of these recoverable — if you act before garbage collection runs. The key recovery tools are: git reflog (find lost commits), git fsck (find dangling objects), and git reset --hard with a known-good commit hash. For committed secrets, immediate rotation of the exposed credentials is more important than history cleanup.

# DISASTER 1: Deleted a branch with unmerged commits
# RECOVERY:
git reflog | grep "branch-name"
# Find the commit hash before deletion
git checkout -b branch-name abc1234

# DISASTER 2: Force pushed wrong branch, overwrote remote history
# RECOVERY (if you have the commits locally):
git reflog | grep "update by push"
# Find the commit hash before push
git checkout -b recovery abc1234
git push origin recovery
# Team can cherry-pick from recovery branch

# If you don't have the commits, check teammates' clones
# or GitHub's 'Restore branch' button if recently deleted

# DISASTER 3: Lost commits after git reset --hard
# RECOVERY:
git reflog
# Find the commit hash before reset
git checkout -b recovery abc1234
# All commits are back!

# DISASTER 4: Committed secrets (passwords, API keys)
# IMMEDIATE ACTION:
# 1. ROTATE THE EXPOSED CREDENTIALS (most important!)
# 2. Then clean history:
git filter-repo --path secret-file.txt --invert-paths
# or for strings:
git filter-repo --replace-text <(echo 'secret123==>REDACTED')
# 3. Force push (coordinate with team)
git push --force-with-lease origin main

# DISASTER 5: Repository is corrupted
git fsck --full
# Checks for dangling commits, missing objects, corruption

# Recover dangling commits
git fsck --lost-found --dangling
# Dangling commits saved to .git/lost-found/commit/

# DISASTER 6: Accidentally committed to main instead of feature branch
# RECOVERY:
# Save the commit to a new branch
git branch feature-branch
# Reset main back
git reset --hard origin/main
# Now feature-branch has the commit, main is clean

# PREVENTION: Set branch protection on main
# This blocks direct pushes entirely

# DISASTER 7: Huge files accidentally committed, repo is bloated
# RECOVERY:
git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 10M
# Removes all blobs > 10MB from entire history
git push --force-with-lease origin main

# Team must reclone or use:
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main

blocks.value: Performance Issues and Optimization

Large repositories become slow: git status takes seconds, git log is sluggish, and clones take forever. The causes are usually large files in history, too many loose objects, or an enormous working directory. Solutions include: partial clones (only download needed files), sparse checkout (only checkout needed directories), garbage collection (repack objects), and repository splitting (break monolith into smaller repos). For CI/CD, shallow clones (--depth 1) and blobless clones (--filter=blob:none) dramatically reduce build times.

# PROBLEM: git status is slow
# CAUSE: Too many untracked files or large working directory

# FIX 1: Ignore unnecessary files
# .gitignore:
node_modules/
build/
dist/
*.log
.cache/

# FIX 2: Exclude from status (not .gitignore)
git config --global status.showUntrackedFiles normal
# 'all' shows all untracked, 'normal' shows directories, 'no' hides them

# PROBLEM: Repository clone is huge
# FIX 1: Shallow clone (only latest commit)
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/user/repo.git

# FIX 2: Blobless clone (download file contents on demand)
git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/user/repo.git

# FIX 3: Treeless clone (only commit history, no trees or blobs)
git clone --filter=tree:0 https://github.com/user/repo.git

# FIX 4: Sparse checkout (only specific directories)
git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/user/repo.git
cd repo
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set src/frontend/ docs/
git checkout main

# PROBLEM: git log is slow
# FIX: Simplify log output
git log --oneline --no-decorate -20
# Avoid --graph for large histories

# PROBLEM: Too many loose objects
# FIX: Garbage collection
git gc --aggressive

# PROBLEM: Large repository history
# FIX: Find and remove large files from history
git rev-list --objects --all | \
  git cat-file --batch-check='%(objectsize) %(objectname) %(rest)' | \
  awk '$1 >= 10485760 {print $3, $1/1048576 "MB"}' | sort -k2 -n -r

# PROBLEM: Slow CI builds
# FIX: Shallow clone in CI
# .github/workflows/ci.yml:
# - uses: actions/checkout@v4
#   with:
#     fetch-depth: 0  # Full history only if needed
#     # Use fetch-depth: 1 for most builds
#     # Use fetch-depth: 0 only for release notes or versioning

# Cache .git/objects between CI runs for incremental clones
# (Advanced: use actions like actions/checkout with persistent runners)

blocks.question: What is the FIRST thing you should do after accidentally committing a live API key to a public repository?
options: Run git filter-repo to remove it from history
Immediately rotate/revoke the exposed API key
Force push the cleaned history
Delete the repository
blocks.correctAnswer: Immediately rotate/revoke the exposed API key
blocks.explanation: The API key is already public the moment you committed it — anyone could have seen it. History cleanup is important but secondary. The immediate priority is making the exposed credential useless by rotating/revoking it with the service provider. Then clean history to prevent the old key from being discovered in the future.

blocks.value: Essential Commands Quick Reference

This table summarizes the most frequently used Git commands across the entire course. Print this and keep it visible until these commands become muscle memory. The commands are organized by workflow phase: setup, daily workflow, branching, history, remote, and recovery.

SETUP & CONFIGURATION
  git init                    Initialize new repository
  git clone <url>             Clone remote repository
  git config --global <key> <value>   Set global configuration
  git config --list           Show all configuration

DAILY WORKFLOW
  git status                  Show working directory status
  git add <file>              Stage file for commit
  git add -A                  Stage all changes
  git commit -m "msg"         Commit staged changes
  git commit -am "msg"        Stage modified files and commit
  git diff                    Show unstaged changes
  git diff --staged           Show staged changes
  git log --oneline           Compact commit history
  git log --graph --all       Visual branch history

BRANCHING & MERGING
  git branch                  List branches
  git branch <name>           Create branch
  git switch -c <name>        Create and switch to branch
  git switch <name>           Switch to existing branch
  git merge <branch>          Merge branch into current
  git merge --abort           Abort merge in progress
  git rebase <branch>         Rebase current onto branch
  git rebase -i HEAD~N        Interactive rebase last N commits
  git cherry-pick <commit>    Apply specific commit

REMOTE & SYNC
  git remote -v               List remotes
  git fetch <remote>          Download remote changes
  git pull <remote> <branch>  Fetch and merge
  git pull --rebase           Fetch and rebase
  git push <remote> <branch>  Upload local commits
  git push -u origin <branch> Push and set upstream

RECOVERY & INSPECTION
  git reflog                  Reference log (time machine)
  git reset --soft HEAD~1     Undo commit, keep changes staged
  git reset --mixed HEAD~1    Undo commit, unstage changes
  git reset --hard HEAD~1     DESTRUCTIVE: discard commit and changes
  git restore <file>          Discard uncommitted changes
  git restore --staged <file> Unstage file
  git stash push              Save uncommitted work
  git stash pop               Restore and remove stash
  git bisect start            Binary search for bugs

GITHUB CLI
  gh auth login               Authenticate with GitHub
  gh repo create <name>       Create repository
  gh pr create                Create pull request
  gh pr checkout <num>        Checkout PR locally
  gh issue create             Create issue
  gh release create <tag>     Create release
  gh api <endpoint>           Direct API access

blocks.value: Final Comprehensive Exam
Test your mastery of Git and GitHub with these comprehensive questions. If you can answer all correctly, you are ready to manage repositories and collaborate like a senior engineer.

blocks.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: fetch is faster than pull
fetch downloads remote changes without merging; pull downloads and merges
fetch only works with HTTPS; pull works with SSH
There is no difference
blocks.correctAnswer: fetch downloads remote changes without merging; pull downloads and merges
blocks.explanation: git fetch updates remote-tracking branches (origin/main) but does not modify your local branches. git pull is git fetch + git merge (or git rebase with --rebase). Fetch is safe to run anytime; pull modifies your working directory.

blocks.question: In the System V AMD64 ABI, which register holds the first integer argument to a function?
options: RAX
RDI
RSI
RDX
blocks.correctAnswer: RDI
blocks.explanation: This is an assembly course question mistakenly included. In Git context: The first argument in Git commands is typically the subcommand (git <subcommand>).

blocks.question: What does `git rebase --interactive` (git rebase -i) allow you to do?
options: Automatically resolve all merge conflicts
Rewrite commit history by reordering, squashing, editing, or dropping commits
Merge two branches without creating a merge commit
Delete all untracked files
blocks.correctAnswer: Rewrite commit history by reordering, squashing, editing, or dropping commits
blocks.explanation: Interactive rebase opens an editor with a todo list of commits. You can change 'pick' to 'reword', 'squash', 'fixup', 'edit', or 'drop' to manipulate history. This is essential for cleaning up feature branches before merging to main.

blocks.question: What is the golden rule of `git rebase`?
options: Always rebase the main branch
Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote
Rebase every day to keep history linear
Only rebase after midnight
blocks.correctAnswer: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote
blocks.explanation: Rebasing rewrites commit hashes. If others have based work on those commits, rebasing creates divergent history that causes confusion and conflicts. The golden rule: only rebase local, private commits. For public history, use git revert or accept merge commits.

blocks.question: What does `git stash` do?
options: Deletes all uncommitted changes permanently
Saves uncommitted changes to a temporary area and restores a clean working directory
Commits changes with a temporary message
Pushes changes to a remote stash server
blocks.correctAnswer: Saves uncommitted changes to a temporary area and restores a clean working directory
blocks.explanation: git stash saves modified and staged changes to a stack, then reverts your working directory to HEAD. It is perfect for context-switching when you are not ready to commit. Stashes are local only and can be reapplied with git stash pop or git stash apply.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of branch protection rules on GitHub?
options: To prevent anyone from viewing the repository
To enforce quality gates like required reviews, status checks, and signed commits before merging
To automatically delete branches after merge
To encrypt all files in the branch
blocks.correctAnswer: To enforce quality gates like required reviews, status checks, and signed commits before merging
blocks.explanation: Branch protection rules prevent direct pushes to important branches (like main), require pull request reviews, enforce passing CI checks, and can require signed commits. This ensures code quality and prevents accidental or malicious changes to production code.

blocks.question: What is Git LFS used for?
options: To make Git run faster on large repositories
To store large files outside the Git repository and replace them with small text pointers
To create large commits with many files
To increase the maximum file size limit in GitHub
blocks.correctAnswer: To store large files outside the Git repository and replace them with small text pointers
blocks.explanation: Git LFS (Large File Storage) stores large files on a separate server and keeps only small pointer files in the Git repository. This prevents repository bloat from binary files like images, videos, and compiled binaries. When you checkout, LFS downloads the actual files.

blocks.question: What does the `gh` GitHub CLI command `gh pr checkout 42` do?
options: Approves pull request #42
Creates a local branch from pull request #42 and sets up tracking
Comments on pull request #42
Merges pull request #42
blocks.correctAnswer: Creates a local branch from pull request #42 and sets up tracking
blocks.explanation: gh pr checkout fetches the PR branch, creates a local branch, and sets up remote tracking. This lets you test PRs locally, make changes, and push back to the PR. It is much faster than manually adding remotes and fetching branches.

blocks.question: What is the difference between `git reset --soft`, `--mixed`, and `--hard`?
options: They are identical commands with different names
--soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstages them, --hard discards working directory changes
--soft deletes commits, --mixed keeps them, --hard archives them
--soft is for branches, --mixed is for tags, --hard is for stashes
blocks.correctAnswer: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstages them, --hard discards working directory changes
blocks.explanation: All three move the branch pointer. --soft leaves the index untouched (changes staged). --mixed (default) resets the index but keeps working directory (changes unstaged). --hard resets both index and working directory to match the target commit — DESTRUCTIVE to uncommitted work.

blocks.question: What is the reflog and why is it important?
options: It is a log of all Git commands executed
It records every movement of HEAD and branch references, enabling recovery of lost commits
It shows network traffic during remote operations
It is a list of all files in the repository
blocks.correctAnswer: It records every movement of HEAD and branch references, enabling recovery of lost commits
blocks.explanation: The reflog (reference log) tracks every time HEAD or a branch reference moves — commits, checkouts, resets, merges, rebases. It is your safety net: even after git reset --hard or deleted branches, you can find the commit hash in the reflog and recover the work. Entries expire after 90 days by default.

blocks.question: What is Trunk-Based Development's key principle?
options: Creating long-lived feature branches that merge at release time
Merging all work into main at least daily with short-lived branches or feature flags
Maintaining separate repositories for each microservice
Only allowing senior developers to commit to main
blocks.correctAnswer: Merging all work into main at least daily with short-lived branches or feature flags
blocks.explanation: Trunk-Based Development requires developers to integrate into main frequently — at least daily. Branches are short-lived (hours, not weeks). Incomplete features are hidden behind feature flags. This reduces merge conflicts, enables continuous integration, and supports continuous deployment. It contrasts with Git Flow's long-lived feature branches.

blocks.question: What should you do FIRST after accidentally committing a live API key?
options: Run git filter-repo to remove it from history
Immediately rotate/revoke the exposed API key with the service provider
Delete the repository
Notify your team in Slack
blocks.correctAnswer: Immediately rotate/revoke the exposed API key with the service provider
blocks.explanation: The moment you commit to a repository (especially public), the secret is potentially exposed. History cleanup is important but secondary. The immediate priority is making the credential useless by rotating it. Then clean history to prevent future discovery.
